title: Edges, vertices, and faces
keyIdea: We describe a 3-D shape by counting its parts. A face is a flat side. An edge is a straight line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner where edges meet (more than one vertex are called vertices). A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A square-based pyramid has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices. A triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices. Some parts are round the back, so turn the shape or look for them.
familyTip: Find a box, such as a cereal box or a dice. Put a small sticker or a blob of play dough on each corner and count them: these are the vertices. Run a finger along each edge, counting as you go. Then turn the box over and count the flat faces. Try the same with a Toblerone-style box (a triangular prism).

visual.caption: Is it a vertex, an edge or a face? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stick a sticker on each vertex, trace every edge, paint and turn a cube, then count a pyramid and a prism.

kid: A 3-D shape is a solid shape you can hold, like a box or a dice. It has parts with special names. A face is a flat side. An edge is a straight line where two faces meet. A vertex is a corner. When there is more than one, we say vertices.
A cube is like a dice. It has 6 faces, and they are all squares. It has 12 edges. It has 8 vertices: 4 on top and 4 at the bottom.

You can not see all of a shape at once. Some faces, edges and corners are at the back. Turn the shape round, or put a sticker on each part as you count it. Then you will not miss one or count one twice.

Different shapes have different numbers. A pyramid with a square bottom has 5 faces, 8 edges and 5 vertices. A triangular prism, like a tent, has 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices. A ball has no edges and no vertices at all.
adult: Ages 6 to 7 (NC Year 2: identify and describe the properties of 3-D shapes, including the number of edges, vertices and faces). Children should use the words face, edge and vertex (plural vertices) correctly, and describe a shape by its numbers: a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

Faces here means flat faces. A cylinder has 2 flat faces and a curved surface, and a sphere has only a curved surface, so it has no edges and no vertices. In the lab all the shapes have flat faces, so every edge is a straight line where two faces meet and every vertex is where edges meet.

Common mistakes: counting only what can be seen, which gives 3 faces for a cube; counting the corners of one face, which gives 4 vertices; counting edges twice or missing the hidden ones; forgetting the base of a pyramid; and mixing up the three words. Marking each part as it is counted stops double counting.

In the lab your child puts a sticker on every vertex of a cube (one is hidden at the back), traces all 12 edges, paints the faces and turns the cube to reach the hidden ones, then counts the vertices of a square-based pyramid and the edges of a triangular prism.

practice.hint: Think of the stickers in the lab. Where did you put them?
practice.explain: A vertex is a corner. The stickers went on the corners of the cube, so a cube has 8 vertices.

practice.prompt: A cube has 6 faces. You have painted {a} of them. How many faces are left to paint?
practice.hint: Start at 6 and take away the faces you have painted.
practice.explain: 6 − {a} = {=6-a}. There are {=6-a} faces left to paint.

practice.prompt: How many edges does a cube have?
practice.hint: Count the edges on top, the edges on the bottom and the edges going up.
practice.explain: 4 on top, 4 on the bottom and 4 going up makes 12 edges.

practice.prompt: A triangular prism has 9 edges. You have traced {a} of them. How many more edges do you need to trace?
practice.hint: Start at 9 and take away the edges you have traced.
practice.explain: 9 − {a} = {=9-a}. You need to trace {=9-a} more edges.

practice.prompt: Tom looks at a cube and says it has 3 faces. Why is he wrong?
choices: Some faces are at the back, so he can not see them
practice.hint: Can you see every side of a box at once?
practice.explain: You can only see 3 faces at once. Turn the cube and you find 3 more: 6 faces in all.

pool.prompt: How many vertices does a cube have?
pool.hint: Count the corners on top and the corners at the bottom.
pool.explain: 4 corners on top and 4 at the bottom make 8 vertices.

pool.prompt: How many faces does a square-based pyramid have?
pool.hint: Count the triangles, then remember the square at the bottom.
pool.explain: 4 triangle faces and 1 square face make 5 faces.

pool.prompt: How many edges does a triangular prism have?
pool.hint: Count the edges on each triangle end, then the edges joining them.
pool.explain: 3 edges on each triangle end makes 6, and 3 more join the ends: 9 edges.

choices: A straight line where two faces meet
pool.hint: Think of tracing in the lab.
pool.explain: An edge is the straight line where two flat faces meet. You traced them in red.

pool.prompt: A cube has 12 edges. {a} of them are painted red and the rest are blue. How many edges are blue?
pool.hint: Start at 12 and take away the red edges.

pool.prompt: Which shape has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices?
pool.hint: Which shape is like a dice?
pool.explain: A cube has 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

pool.prompt: How many vertices does a ball (a sphere) have?
pool.hint: Does a ball have any corners?
pool.explain: A sphere is curved all over. It has no corners, so it has 0 vertices and 0 edges.

pool.prompt: A square-based pyramid has 5 vertices. You have put stickers on {a} of them. How many stickers do you still need?
pool.hint: Start at 5 and take away the stickers you have already used.

pool.prompt: How can you make sure you count every vertex of a box, and none twice?
choices: Put a sticker on each one as you count it
Only count the ones at the front
pool.hint: What did you do in the lab?
pool.explain: Marking each vertex as you count it means you do not miss the ones at the back or count one twice.
